section_title: What can Christ cleanse that the earlier rites could not?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 11 But when Christ came as high priest of the good things that have come, He went through the greater and more perfect tabernacle that is not made by hands and is not a part of this creation. 12 He did not enter by the blood of goats and calves, but He entered the Most Holy Place once for all by His own blood, thus securing eternal redemption.

13 For if the blood of goats and bulls and the ashes of a heifer sprinkled on those who are ceremonially unclean sanctify them so that their bodies are clean, 14 how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered Himself unblemished to God, purify our consciences from works of death, so that we may serve the living God!

context_lines: The contrast now reaches Christ. He enters the greater sanctuary through His own blood, securing eternal redemption. Unlike the repeated animal offerings, His entrance is once for all.

The comparison with a heifer’s ashes refers to the cleansing described in [Numbers 19](https://biblehub.com/bsb/numbers/19.htm), including cleansing after contact with a dead body. These rites restored people to the cleanliness required for worship. Hebrews uses their recognized role to explain how much greater Christ’s work is.

Christ offered Himself unblemished to God. His blood means His life given in sacrifice, not a separate substance detached from His willing offering. The cleansing reaches the conscience and frees people from works of death so that they can serve the living God.

The word [translated serve](https://biblehub.com/greek/3000.htm) describes religious service or worship. Here the writer’s emphasis falls on what cleansing makes possible: a life turned toward God. It is more than relief from guilt with no change of direction.
common_interpretation_lines: [Calvin](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/hebrews/9.htm), [Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-epistle-to-the-hebrews/) and the [USCCB notes](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/hebrews/9) agree that Christ provides the lasting cleansing the earlier rites could not supply on their own, and that this cleansing leads to service.

They differ over two details. Calvin and Wesley understand the greater tabernacle in verse 11 as Christ’s body, through which He entered heaven; the USCCB notes identify it with the heavenly sanctuary. For the eternal Spirit in verse 14, Calvin and Wesley understand the Holy Spirit’s work in Christ’s offering. The USCCB note instead understands the expression as Christ’s enduring risen life. These are interpretations of the wording, not reasons to obscure the shared emphasis on Christ’s unblemished offering.
god_plan_lines: [Titus 2:11–14](https://biblehub.com/bsb/titus/2.htm) connects Christ giving Himself to redeem a people with their eagerness to do good. [Ephesians 2:8–10](https://biblehub.com/bsb/ephesians/2.htm) likewise joins salvation by grace with the good works God prepares for His people.

This gives the cleansing its place in the larger purpose of redemption. God rescues people into life with Him, where they can love and serve. Their service follows His saving work; it does not supply what His sacrifice lacked.
current_position_lines: Our study [Worship as the Early Church Knew It](https://thewayofscripture.com/studies/worship.html) understands this verse as forgiveness leading into a life of service to God. Christ cleanses people so that they can serve Him with a purified heart. That service reaches into daily obedience and care for others, beyond the time spent in a gathering.
